headline: 12 hours on camera, building outreach so personal it looks impossible to automate
paragraphs: This hackathon has one audience: your company. I come from marketing and have freelanced for ten years, and I've spent the last nine months on an AI sabbatical doing nothing but building with Claude Code. Now I want to apply that inside a real company, with a real CRM and real IT restrictions. So I'm spending 12 hours of recorded time building, in public and from scratch, what a GTM engineer builds: automated workflows that feed your pipeline. I could replay things I've built before, but I'm building it live so you can watch how I think. Keep in mind that once it's built, it's built. The personalization you watch me do by hand could run for every key account in your CRM.

The idea behind it is knowledge arbitrage. Before AI, outreach meant choosing between personalization and volume. You could research a prospect deeply, but that took so long you could only do it for a few key accounts. Or you could send the same message to a lot of people. Most teams chose volume, and at the time that was the right call. Recipients could always tell which one they were getting, so real personalization was a costly signal. What's new is that you no longer have to choose, and most people don't know that yet.

Most AI outreach today is high volume and low quality. The opening is AI so good it reads as human: a message so tailored that the recipient assumes you spent three days on it, when an agent ran in the background for a couple of hours. This hackathon really is costly for me today, but once it's automated, the same effort could go to your top 100 accounts. It won't be free. It costs tokens, the first version will run on the expensive side, and the work after the build is making it better and cheaper, teaching your people to use it, and upgrading it as things change. And if you want to bring in AI without cutting half the team, the pipeline is the first place to put it, because your people get more done while more work comes in.

Here's what this site will fill up with as the hackathon goes on: a few articles on the core ideas, including why nothing in inbound compares to what outbound with AI can now do, my background, and live demos. Instead of service pages, there'll be a page for each person likely to be involved in hiring me, built from deep research into your org chart, with a pitch for their likely top concerns and the parts of these recordings that matter to them. The goal is to make this one of the easiest hiring decisions your company has made: proof of what I can do instead of a CV, and a deal where I won't ask for a lot of money. If it looks rough when you first visit, it is. Check back every couple of hours and watch it come together.
